lead: An engine burns a mixture of petrol and air, and the air-fuel ratio decides how completely the fuel burns and what leaves the tailpipe: carbon monoxide (CO), unburnt hydrocarbons (HC) and nitrogen oxides (NOx). No single ratio is best everywhere, so the controller moves between rich, stoichiometric and lean as the engine starts, warms, cruises and accelerates. This chapter links the mixture to the pollutants, the oxidising and three-way catalysts, exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) and fuel economy in km/L, L/100 km and grams of CO₂ per km.
prereq: You need: the legal ceilings from emission norms, and first-year chemistry of complete and incomplete combustion.

sections.h3: Air-fuel ratio, lambda and the pollutants

blocks.text: Petrol needs about 14.7 kg of air for every 1 kg of fuel to burn completely. This is the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio, AFR<sub>st</sub>. The actual air-fuel ratio AFR is air mass divided by fuel mass. Lambda (λ), the excess-air ratio, compares the two.

blocks.where: AFR is the actual ratio in kg of air per kg of petrol; AFR<sub>st</sub> = 14.7 for petrol; λ has no unit. λ = 1 is stoichiometric, λ < 1 is rich (too little air for the fuel) and λ > 1 is lean (excess air).

blocks.text: Each pollutant follows λ in its own way.

items: CO forms when carbon burns with too little oxygen, so it rises steeply on the rich side and is very low lean.

HC is fuel that escaped the flame: quenched at the cold cylinder wall, hidden in crevices round the piston rings, or never burnt. It is high when rich, lowest slightly lean, and rises again very lean, when the flame starts to misfire.

NOx forms when nitrogen and oxygen combine at high flame temperature. It needs both heat and spare oxygen, so it is low rich, peaks slightly lean (about λ = 1.05 to 1.1) and falls again very lean because the flame is cooler.
In a diesel, PM (soot) comes from fuel-rich pockets inside the spray, even though the average diesel mixture is lean.

sections.h3: Catalytic converters and exhaust gas recirculation

blocks.text: A catalytic converter is a ceramic or metal honeycomb in the exhaust, coated with a porous washcoat that carries precious metals (platinum and palladium for oxidation, rhodium for NOx reduction). An oxidising (two-way) catalyst uses spare oxygen in the exhaust to burn CO and HC. It lowers CO and HC but cannot remove NOx.

items: Oxidation: 2CO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub>; for a hydrocarbon C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>m</sub>: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>m</sub> + (n + m/4) O<sub>2</sub> → n CO<sub>2</sub> + (m/2) H<sub>2</sub>O.

blocks.text: A three-way catalyst does both jobs at once, but only in a narrow window around λ = 1, about 1 percent wide. Lean of the window the spare oxygen leaves NOx unreduced; rich of it there is too little oxygen to burn all the CO and HC. Conversion efficiency is (pollutant in − pollutant out) ÷ pollutant in.

The catalyst must also be hot. Its light-off temperature, where conversion reaches about half, is about 250 to 350 °C. In the first minute after a cold start the catalyst is below light-off, so that minute can carry much of a short trip's emissions. The ECU therefore retards the spark to send hotter exhaust to the catalyst (see spark timing control), and some engines pump secondary air into the exhaust.

EGR, exhaust gas recirculation, sends a metered part of the exhaust back to the intake. The inert gas dilutes the charge and lowers peak flame temperature, so NOx falls. At part load, moderate EGR has little effect on fuel economy and can improve it slightly, because the engine needs less throttling (lower pumping loss). Too much EGR slows the burn, raises HC and causes misfire. The ECU schedules EGR by speed and load and shuts it at idle and full load.

sections.h3: Spark timing, fuel economy and CO₂

blocks.text: Spark timing also moves the emissions. Retarding the spark from the best-torque point lowers peak temperature, so NOx falls, and leaves the exhaust hotter, which burns more HC in the exhaust. The cost is torque, so fuel use per km rises.

Fuel economy has two common forms. km per litre is higher-is-better; litres per 100 km is lower-is-better. They are reciprocal: L/100 km = 100 ÷ (km/L). A car giving 14.7 km/L uses 100 ÷ 14.7 = 6.8 L/100 km.

CO₂ is not a product of bad combustion: almost all the carbon in the fuel leaves as CO₂ when the burn is good. So CO₂ per km is fixed by fuel used per km. Burning 1 kg of petrol makes about 3.16 kg of CO₂; with a density of 0.74 kg/L that is about 2.34 kg of CO₂ per litre. Cutting CO₂ means cutting fuel.

The controller chooses a compromise at every operating point. Steady cruise runs at λ = 1 in closed loop, so the three-way catalyst can clean all three pollutants (see electronic fuel control). Full load runs slightly rich (λ about 0.85 to 0.9) for power and to cool the exhaust valves and catalyst. Cold start runs rich until the fuel evaporates well. Deceleration cuts fuel completely. The effect of each choice on torque and fuel use is measured as in torque, power and BSFC.

examples.question: A car uses 6.8 L of petrol to cover 100 km. Petrol density is 0.74 kg/L and burning 1 kg of petrol makes 3.16 kg of CO₂. Find (a) the economy in km/L, (b) the fuel mass per km, (c) the CO₂ in g/km, and (d) λ when the air-fuel ratio drops to 13.2:1 during hard acceleration.
steps: (b) Fuel mass per 100 km = 6.8 L × 0.74 kg/L = 5.032 kg, so fuel mass per km = 5.032 ÷ 100 = 0.05032 kg/km.
(d) λ = 13.2 ÷ 14.7 = 0.898, about 0.90. Since λ < 1 the mixture is rich: CO and HC rise and NOx falls while it lasts.
examples.answer: 14.71 km/L; 0.0503 kg of petrol per km; 159 g CO₂/km; at 13.2:1, λ = 0.90 (rich).
examples.check:
v, d = 6.8, 0.74
print(round(100/v, 2))
print(round(v*d/100, 4))
print(round(v*d/100*3.16*1000, 1))
print(round(13.2/14.7, 2))

examples.question: On the test cycle a petrol car makes, before the catalyst, CO 8.0 g/km, HC 1.2 g/km and NOx 1.0 g/km. With the catalyst hot and λ held at 1, conversion is CO 90 %, HC 92 %, NOx 95 %. (a) Find the tailpipe values and compare them with BS VI (CO 1.0, HC 0.10, NOx 0.06 g/km). (b) A faulty sensor makes the engine run at λ = 1.02, where NOx conversion falls to 60 %. Find the new tailpipe NOx.
steps: CO: 8.0 × (1 − 0.90) = 0.80 g/km, under 1.0. HC: 1.2 × (1 − 0.92) = 0.096 g/km, under 0.10. NOx: 1.0 × (1 − 0.95) = 0.05 g/km, under 0.06. The car passes, with HC only 4 % under its ceiling.
At λ = 1.02 the spare oxygen stops the NOx reduction: NOx = 1.0 × (1 − 0.60) = 0.40 g/km.
0.40 ÷ 0.06 = 6.7 times the limit. A 2 % lean drift fails the car, which is why the ECU holds λ = 1 in closed loop.
examples.answer: Tailpipe CO 0.80, HC 0.096, NOx 0.05 g/km: a pass. At λ = 1.02 NOx rises to 0.40 g/km, 6.7 times the BS VI limit.

traps: Treating λ and AFR as the same number. λ has no unit; AFR is kg of air per kg of fuel. λ = 1 means AFR = 14.7 for petrol, not 1:1.
Believing a three-way catalyst cleans any mixture. Outside its window near λ = 1, CO and HC (rich) or NOx (lean) pass through.
Forgetting light-off. A cold catalyst does almost nothing even at λ = 1; about 250 to 350 °C is needed.
Saying an oxidising catalyst removes NOx. It only burns CO and HC; NOx needs the reducing step of a three-way catalyst.
Listing CO₂ with the products of poor combustion. CO₂ comes from good combustion and is fixed by the fuel burnt; CO and HC come from poor combustion.

quiz.q: Define the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio of petrol and the excess-air ratio λ.
quiz.a: AFR<sub>st</sub> ≈ 14.7 kg of air per kg of petrol, the ratio for complete burning. λ = AFR ÷ AFR<sub>st</sub>, so λ = 1 at the stoichiometric mixture.

quiz.q: Why does NOx peak slightly lean of λ = 1 rather than rich?
quiz.a: NOx needs high flame temperature and spare oxygen. A rich mixture has no spare oxygen; a very lean flame is cooler. Both conditions are met best slightly lean, about λ = 1.05 to 1.1.

quiz.q: A car uses 7.5 L/100 km. Petrol density is 0.74 kg/L and 1 kg of petrol makes 3.16 kg of CO₂. Find g CO₂/km.
Why does a three-way catalyst fail outside the λ = 1 window?
quiz.a: Lean exhaust has spare oxygen, so NOx is not reduced. Rich exhaust lacks oxygen, so CO and HC are not fully oxidised. Only near λ = 1 are both reactions supplied at once.

quiz.q: How does EGR lower NOx, and what does it do to fuel economy?
quiz.a: The recirculated inert gas dilutes the charge and lowers peak flame temperature. At part load moderate EGR has little effect on economy and can improve it slightly by reducing throttling; too much EGR slows the burn, causes misfire and then costs fuel.

quiz.q: What is the light-off temperature of a catalyst?
quiz.a: The temperature at which conversion reaches about half; about 250 to 350 °C for a petrol catalyst.

quiz.q: An engine runs at AFR 15.5:1. Find λ and say whether the mixture is rich or lean.
quiz.a: λ = 15.5 ÷ 14.7 = 1.054. Since λ > 1 the mixture is lean.

quiz.q: Engine-out NOx is 0.8 g/km and the limit is 0.06 g/km. What conversion efficiency must the catalyst reach?
quiz.a: Allowed out = 0.06, so conversion ≥ (0.8 − 0.06) ÷ 0.8 = 0.925, that is 92.5 %. Only a hot three-way catalyst held at λ = 1 reaches this.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines use wideband lambda sensors, catalysts mounted close to the engine for fast light-off, gasoline particulate filters and cooled EGR. CO₂ rules push downsized turbo engines, stop-start and 48 V mild hybrids. Research covers lean NOx traps for lean-burn petrol and real-driving emission control. Search next for "three-way catalyst window", "catalyst light-off" and "cooled EGR".

figure.caption: How CO, HC and NOx in the raw exhaust change with λ (a trend sketch). The worked example's 13.2 : 1 mixture sits on the rich side at λ = 0.90; the three-way catalyst works only in the narrow shaded window at λ = 1.

spec.aria: Curves against lambda from 0.8 to 1.2: CO high when rich and falling, HC lowest slightly lean and rising at both ends, NOx peaking near lambda 1.06, a narrow window at lambda 1, and the worked example point at lambda 0.90.
